summary: Daniel Liss, founder and CEO of the disposable camera social network Dispo, argues in a TechCrunch contributed piece that the FTC's refiled antitrust case against Facebook should succeed. He contends the FTC must define the market as personal social networking including messaging, measure share by revenue rather than time spent or users, and can alternatively argue Facebook suppresses creator wages. He compares Facebook's creator payouts unfavorably with YouTube's and frames Facebook as a modern Standard Oil.
one_line: Daniel Liss argues the FTC's refiled case against Facebook should succeed by using a messaging-inclusive market and revenue-based share, plus a creator-wage harm theory.
key_facts: Daniel Liss is the founder and CEO of Dispo, the digital disposable camera social network.
The FTC refiled its case to dismantle Facebook's monopoly on the day Mark Zuckerberg appeared on national TV to make a 'special announcement'.
Judge James E. Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia wrote that 'No one who hears the title of the 2010 film The Social Network wonders which company it is about.'
Liss argues the FTC must define the market as personal social networking, which includes messaging.
Liss argues the FTC must establish that Facebook controls over 60% of the market, with revenue as the correct metric.
Liss states that Facebook controls over 90% of the personal social networking market by revenue, citing Snapchat's investor presentation.
Liss says WhatsApp and Messenger have over 2 billion and 1.3 billion users respectively.
Liss argues Boasberg is confusing business model with market when he says revenues earned from advertising cannot measure personal networking share.
Liss notes YouTube's traditional creator revenue share is 55%.
YouTube announced it has paid $30 billion to creators and rights holders over the last three years.
Liss estimates YouTube paid creators about $5 billion annually, a third of its roughly $46 billion revenue over that period.
Facebook announced a $1 billion creator program over a year and change, which Liss calls a paltry sum.
Liss says Facebook has generated $210 billion in revenue over the equivalent three-year period, and one-third paid to creators would be $70 billion.
Liss cites Lina Khan's 2017 note that began the New Brandeis movement as arguing the traditional consumer harm test does not adequately address Big Tech harms.
Liss concludes that under the Sherman Act monopolies are illegal in and of themselves and consumer harm is not a necessary condition.
